verdicts.note: Matches Theobald's gloss in Furness ('stood cap in hand, soliciting him'). 'Hat in hand' carries both the doffed cap and the humble petition, and it removes the modern 'hats off to him' = admiration misreading. Natural by ear.

Literal rendering of the unresolved crux (Schmidt calls it an 'unintelligible passage'; no emendation is accepted). It restores 'almost', and 'beautiful' for 'fair', and adds nothing. 'By' is the natural modern preposition for 'damn'd in'. Record the crux choice (rule 7).

Schmidt and Onions give 'spinster' only as 'one who spins'. Dropping 'old maid' removes the later spinster sense and the added age and marital status. 'A woman at her spinning wheel' keeps Iago's gendered sneer (spinning was women's work) and reads naturally.

In the original, 'his eyes' is Othello's, and the 'he' just before is Cassio, so v1's 'his own eyes' misled. 'The general' names the referent without inventing anything, and it is Iago's natural word for his commander. It is a referent, not an editor's aside.

Schmidt: 'serve the turn = to answer the purpose' (cites this line), and 'upon' in its hostile sense ('a plot of death upon him'). 'Serve my own ends against him' translates the idiom, keeps the serve/serve echo and keeps the malice.
Schmidt: cashier = 'to discard from service'. 'Dismissed' is exact and register-neutral, and it matches 'dismiss' for 'cast' at 1.40.
Restores the original's structure: 'we come to do you service' and 'you think we are ruffians' jointly lead to the consequence. Grammatical and clear by ear.

Explicitly checked: removing '— having sex' is right. The image explains itself (a coupled pair forming one beast with two backs), and the idiom is still current. The listener has just heard 'an old black ram is mounting your white ewe' (1.20) and 'your daughter covered by a Barbary stallion' (1.31), and Brabantio's 'You're a villain' shows the insult landed. The tag was a footnote-style aside that the standard's Target forbids. It turned Iago's gleeful obscenity into a clinical explanation, which blunts rather than keeps the bawdy (rule 5), and it diluted a famous, already-clear line (rule 2). The bawdy loses no strength, and the v2 sentence is natural.

'Of here and everywhere' sneers at a man who belongs to no fixed place. Warburton (Furness) glosses the related 'erring Barbarian' as 'a vagabond, one that has no house nor country', and M. Mason ties it to this line. 'Here one day and anywhere the next' makes the sneer audible, where v1's 'belongs here and everywhere' sounded like praise. It adds no fact and stays inside unit [15,17].

The colon turns the dangling 'that' clause into an explanation of the 'loud and pressing reasons', and 'for their souls' keeps its idiomatic 'to save their souls'. Clear by ear, and nothing crosses into the next unit.
Natural modern order with the same sense: don't judge daughters' minds by their visible actions.

Implements G1's recommended wording exactly, on Johnson's reading. In Furness, Johnson says Brabantio's voice 'would turn the balance as effectually as the Duke's'. 'In practice' renders 'in his effect' (by weight and influence, not by law). 'Double' moves to line 7 but stays inside unit [5,8]. Record the crux choice.
Completes E12. 'His word carries double weight, as much as the duke's' states the equal comparison, so the listener no longer takes away that Brabantio outweighs the Duke.

Adopts the standard reading of the 'unbonneted' crux: Onions has 'uncovered, (hence) on equal terms', and Theobald and Coleridge in Furness read it as 'without the symbol of a petitioning inferior'. It removes the garbled 'speak for themselves' splice and keeps the hat image together with its point. Record the crux choice.
'Just as ... so' restores the correlative that 'since' had made causal. Changing 'just' to 'simply' avoids a doubled 'just'. The 'also' is slightly redundant but harmless.

Not an invention. The source prints '[_To Brabantio._]' at the head of this line (pg1531 l.697), and Tinct's original edition drops inline stage directions, so the vocative restores a cue the play has. A name in front is ordinary speech, not a footnote, and it corrects the addressee before 'I didn't see you'. Pairing it with 'noble sir' is idiomatic.
Schmidt, abuse sense 9 'to deceive'. It fits Brabantio's triad (deceived by spells, stolen, corrupted) and removes the modern assault reading.
'Bloody' here means blood-shedding: the code of capital punishments. 'The law's deadly book' keeps that sense and removes the swear-word reading, and 'harshest letter' still renders 'bitter letter'.

Grounded in the source's '[_To Othello._]' (pg1531 l.744), which the Tinct original omits. The vocative lets the listener hear that Brabantio's 'Nothing, but this is so' interrupts a question put to Othello. Natural, not footnote-like.
Famous and already clear: 'potent', 'grave' and 'reverend' are all current English, so the recognizable line is restored (rule 2). 'Lords' for 'signiors' is fine.
Schmidt, pith 2 'strength, force' (cites this line). The image of the arms and their strength is kept, and 'since I was seven' is implied. Matches G1's proposal.
Famous, clear phrase restored. 'Plain' still renders 'round' (Schmidt: round = plain, blunt).
'And for her ... to fall in love with ...!' is a grammatical modern exclamatory infinitive. The dashes make the list a parenthesis that the ear can hold.
'Saying so is no proof' removes the 'claiming that this isn't proof' misparse. 'Vouch' = assert.
Natural order for 'as truly as ... so justly', and 'grave ears' is restored. The bracket wrapper of this continuation paragraph is intact.

Removes the fronted object. All the content is carried (antres, idle deserts, quarries, rocks, hills touching heaven, 'hint' = occasion), and the following 'and of the cannibals' still attaches to 'speak of'.
'Lean in earnestly' carries both the physical and the attentive sense of 'incline', and the right sense of 'seriously' (= in earnest).

Furness: Lettsom reads 'intentively' here as 'all at a stretch, or so as to comprehend the story as a whole', and Furness endorses it; Steevens has 'with attention to all its parts'. 'Never from start to finish' is that sense, and it removes v1's contradiction with 'greedy ear'. It sits well after 'in full'.

Schmidt glosses 'hint' in this line as 'occasion', and 'taking that hint' carries both the occasion and her suggestion. The full stop makes 'She loved me ...' heard as the summary to the Senate. 'Spoke up' = declared himself.
Matches the source's full stop after 'husband'. The new boundary between [3,5] and [6,9] corresponds.
The capitalized new sentence is consistent with E30, and the 'so much ... so much' comparison is carried whole in [6,9].
Natural order, keeping both 'with all my heart' clauses for the paradox. The dash still marks the turn to Desdemona.

The pun is attested. In Furness (on 'free comfort'), Johnson glosses the comfort as 'moral precepts ... liberally bestowed on occasion of the sentence', which is the verdict sense. The Duke's 'sentence' is 'a wise saying' at 3.51, so the listener can connect both senses. The short appositive is the standard's sanctioned pun device (rule 4), not a stray footnote. 'Takes' replaces the first 'bears', but 'bear' survives twice.
Reattaches the relative clause to its head, and keeps 'sentence' for the pun set up in E33. The long subject is still manageable by ear.
'Most grave senators' is consistent with E20 and E25.
Restores the original's agent: the charter found in the Duke's voice is what assists her. 'Charter' (= privilege, warrant) is current English and not a false friend here.

Reattaches 'I love him for' to 'rites'. The appositive keeps both senses audible (rites of love, rights of a wife), covering Keightley's 'amorous rites' and Warburton's 'rights' in Furness. The gloss content is unchanged from v1; only its place moved.

Schmidt: seel = 'to close up the eyes, to blind (originally a term of falconry)'; speculative instruments = 'my eye'; officed = 'having a place or function'. The falconer simile unpacks 'seel' inside the sentence rather than as an aside. 'Blinding the faculties that serve my duties' keeps both instruments under 'seel', and the sentence runs cleanly into 'so that my pleasures corrupt ...'.
Removes the 'giving orders to spend' misparse.
Roderigo has only said 'Iago —', so 'What is it?' is the right sense of 'What sayst thou'.

Onions glosses guinea-hen at this line as 'strumpet' (Schmidt has only 'a term of contempt for a woman'). 'Tart' matches that cant register and strength without adding obscenity, and dropping 'silly little' removes the softening. In the 'X of a Y' frame 'tart' is the referent, so a pastry reading is unlikely.
'Come on' now stands where it belongs, and the purpose phrase is joined to its verb.
Text unchanged. The new boundary between [1,4] and [5,6] corresponds exactly to 'Even till we make ... An indistinct regard'.
Restores the subject ('and who'). 'Clever flourishes of poets' praise' renders 'quirks of blazoning pens'.
The merged unit reads naturally and carries every item.
Famous line restored. 'Critical' = censorious is also the current sense.

Implements G1. The white/wight appositive was inaudible (homophones) and used banned single-quote scare marks, while 'a white man' carries both senses. 'In bed' keeps the bawdy 'fit' audible for Desdemona's 'Worse and worse' and adds no obscenity.
Schmidt: Paradox = 'an absurdity', citing this line.
Keeps the 'small beer' image (rule 2) with a brief in-sentence gloss that US listeners need.
Personified Death keeps Othello's hyperbole and avoids the stock phrase.
Text unchanged. The new boundary after 'nature,' corresponds to the original's semicolon.
Natural order. The parenthesis mirrors the original's own parenthesis and is not a gloss.
Restores 'poisonous mineral' (a corrosive such as arsenic).
Restores 'at least', Iago's fallback qualification.

Implements G1. 'Trash' is the text as printed (Steevens; Schmidt records the modern editors' 'to restrain a dog by a trash'). The appositive keeps the deliberate jingle and explains the hunting sense on the spot, like the standard's 'lie, meaning sleep'. The modern 'trash' verb misreading is corrected at once, and line 18 completes the sentence.
'Revelry' renders 'revels' in the herald's register.
Spelling only (honourable to honorable).
Spelling only (offence to offense).
The resumptive 'them' after the dash makes the fronted object followable by ear. honour to honor is folded in, and all content is carried.
Spelling only (offence to offense).
Spelling only (judgement to judgment).
Spelling only (offence to offense).
Removes the slang 'loser', and 'as having lost it' is the sense of 'repute yourself such a loser'.

Schmidt lists this very line under familiar 'attached and serviceable to men', grouped with 'familiar spirits'. Coming right after Cassio's 'devil', 'familiar' keeps the spirit pun without an appended gloss.
Schmidt glosses 'parallel' in this line as 'conformable to the purpose'. 'One that runs in line with his aim' unpacks it inside the sentence, keeping the image and making its point.
Restores the do/undo antithesis. 'Undo her credit' is heard as 'ruin her standing'.
Removes the modern slang and matches the 6.57 rendering. The bracket wrapper is intact.
Makes the tale/tail pun audible, which the next two speeches depend on ('What tale hangs by it' / 'the kind that blows from behind'). A clown's jokey expansion suits his register.

Spelling only (favour to favor). Related miss: 7.19 (Clown) still has British 'endeavour'. It is the only -our spelling left anywhere in v2, because the normalizer's word list omits it; change it to 'endeavor'.
Removes the duplicated request. 'Arrange for me to have some access to' = 'procure me some access'.
G1's optional polish on Malone's reading. The bracket wrapper is intact.

summary: 71 verdicts: 71 accept, 0 revise, 0 reject. 1.33 (E8): removing '— having sex' is confirmed. The image is self-explanatory, and it is prepared by 1.20 and 1.31. The tag was a footnote-style aside that flattened Iago's obscenity. Every gloss claim in the edit reasons was checked against Schmidt, Onions or Furness, and each holds: off-capp'd (Theobald), serve my turn, pith, intentively (Lettsom), hint, seel/speculative/officed, guinea-hen (Onions 'strumpet'), paradox, parallel, familiar, trash (Steevens), the 'sentence' pun (Johnson) and 'as double as' (Johnson). Every G1-sourced AFTER matches G1's proposed wording. Added names: 'Brabantio —' (3.24) and 'Othello,' (3.33) are grounded in the source's [_To Brabantio._] and [_To Othello._] stage directions, which the Tinct original edition drops. They are vocatives, not footnotes. 'The general's' (1.4) only names the referent. House-style edits E57, E58, E60, E61, E62 and E69 change spelling only. One miss remains: 'endeavour' at 7.19, the only -our spelling left in v2 (the normalizer's list lacks it). Crux choices to record (rule 7): 1.4 'almost damn'd in a fair wife' (received text, literal); 2.3 'as double as' (Johnson: equal to the Duke's); 2.4 'unbonneted' (Onions/Theobald: on equal terms); 4.105 'trash' (Steevens). Re-cut units: all 28 paragraphs are contiguous and gapless on both sides, and every modern span corresponds to its original span with nothing crossing a boundary. No unit problems.
